title: The Discovery of Penicillin
subtitle: Fleming, 1928
subject: sciences
description: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold had killed the bacteria on a culture dish. That accident produced the first great antibiotic.

hero.hook: A forgotten dish, a patch of mold, and medicine changes forever.

blocks.text: Before antibiotics, a simple infection could kill. A cut, a case of pneumonia, a battlefield wound: the body often had to fight alone.
In **1928**, the Scottish doctor **Alexander Fleming** stumbled on a substance that could kill bacteria. It would be called **penicillin**. But turning it into a real medicine took years more.
Fleming was studying bacteria in London. Back from vacation, he looked over some old culture dishes. On one of them, a **mold** had grown. All around it, the bacteria were dead.

blocks.caption: Fleming and the key idea: something in the mold stops bacteria

blocks.text: The mold belonged to the genus **Penicillium**. Fleming realized that it produced an antibacterial substance, and he named it penicillin. But he could never purify enough of it to treat patients.
Fleming said later that if he had been tidier, he would have thrown the dish away. A messy lab helped the discovery along.

sections.title: Oxford turns the idea into a cure

blocks.text: In the early **1940s**, at Oxford, **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** picked up the work. With their team, they isolated penicillin, concentrated it, and tested it on animals and then on humans.
The Second World War made the job urgent: infected soldiers had to be treated. Penicillin went from a lab curiosity to a strategic asset.

blocks.caption: New industrial methods had to be invented just to grow the mold

blocks.text: Treating millions of people meant producing enormous quantities. The United States industrialized production during the war. Giant tanks grew the mold much the way a brewery makes beer.
In **1945**, Fleming, Florey and Chain received the Nobel Prize. Medicine entered the age of antibiotics.
Today, too many antibiotics badly used have let some bacteria turn **resistant**: the drugs no longer kill them. Fleming had warned about that risk long before.

Penicillin came out of an accident Fleming noticed in **1928**, then became a medicine thanks to Florey, Chain and the wartime industry. It has saved millions of lives, so long as we do not wear it out.
